analysis.one_liner: Bans federal agencies from requiring free public access to taxpayer-funded research they finance.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in December 2011 and referred to the House Oversight Committee, it received no further action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred any federal agency from requiring that research it pays for be made freely available online if a commercial or nonprofit journal publisher had contributed editing or peer review. In practice, it would have protected the paywall business of academic journal publishers against public-access policies like the one at the National Institutes of Health, which requires that NIH-funded papers be posted to a free public database within a year. Taxpayers would have had to buy back, often one article at a time, the results of research their taxes already funded.
analysis.who_benefits: Academic journal publishers, whose subscription paywalls and per-article fees would be protected by law; agencies could never mandate that publicly funded papers be released free online without the publisher's consent.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any federal agency from adopting, maintaining, or continuing any policy that permits network dissemination of a 'private-sector research work' without the prior consent of its publisher, locking in the publisher's control over who can read the paper and at what price.

It also bars agencies from requiring authors, or their employers, to agree to online release of their papers, removing the mechanism public-access mandates use to build free archives of federally funded research.

The definition of 'private-sector research work' covers any version of an article on federally funded research to which a commercial or nonprofit publisher has contributed value such as peer review or editing, sweeping in nearly all journal-published science and excluding only raw data and routine progress reports.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, patients, and researchers, who would have had to pay again to read results of research their taxes funded; libraries and universities footing rising subscription bills would also bear the cost.

drawbacks.text: Publishers argue that peer review, editing, and journal infrastructure add real value and cost money, and that a government mandate to give the results away free threatens the financial model that supports those services.

An honest supporter would also acknowledge that the bill went far beyond protecting any single policy: it would have stripped agencies of the power to adopt any future public-access rule, entrenching private paywalls over taxpayer-funded work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The publishers' point about the cost of peer review has some merit, but the bill's remedy was disproportionate: rather than paying publishers for a service, it would have made it illegal for agencies to let the public read work the public already paid for. The bill was written to protect one industry's revenue stream at the expense of everyone who funds, performs, or relies on publicly financed science.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee from the day it was introduced; the committee never acted, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Darrell Issa introduced the bill on December 16, 2011, joined by Representative Carolyn Maloney, and it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
The bill's only action was that referral; the committee took up no markup and the House never voted on it.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died with it, so no federal agency was ever barred from releasing publicly funded research online.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers, patients, and researchers kept the ability of federal agencies to make publicly funded research freely available; publishers did not get the legal lock on paywalls they sought, though the existing paywall system also remained in place.

for.name: Darrell Issa
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-CA); bill sponsor and chair of the Oversight and Government Reform Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Research Works Act and referred it to his own committee, which took no further action on it.

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Joined Issa as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill in the thirteen months before Congress ended.

against.name: Elsevier and major academic publishers
against.what_they_did: After a researcher boycott campaign drew national attention to the bill, publicly withdrew their support for it in early 2012.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan but tiny — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no roll-call vote was ever taken; it died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have written the publishers' paywall model into law, barring agencies from requiring that publicly funded papers be released free without the publisher's consent. Their gain — subscription fees and per-article charges for publicly financed research — would have come directly at the public's cost.

Researchers would have lost the ability to deposit their own federally funded papers in open archives, and universities and libraries would have kept paying rising subscription and per-article fees for work produced largely on their campuses and in their labs.
